props.title: In the Valley of Elah

sections.content: In the Valley of Elah represents a pivotal moment in post-9/11 cinema, with Tommy Lee Jones delivering a devastating portrayal of a veteran father investigating his son's murder after returning from Iraq. The film joins other critical Iraq War examinations like The Hurt Locker (2009) and Stop-Loss (2008) in exploring the psychological toll of modern warfare. Director Paul Haggis strips away Hollywood glamorization, presenting a raw meditation on how war transforms soldiers and the families they leave behind.

sections.content: The film's procedural elements echo earlier military investigation films like A Few Good Men (1992) and Basic (2003), but Haggis grounds the story in devastating realism. The handheld camera footage from soldiers' phones presaged the role digital media would play in documenting modern warfare, something later explored in films like Redacted (2007) and Lions for Lions (2007).

Tommy Lee Jones's performance as Hank Deerfield stands alongside other powerful portrayals of military family members like The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) and Coming Home (1978). His stoic exterior cracking under the weight of grief became a template for later war-impact films like Last Flag Flying (2017) and Thank You for Your Service (2017). SUBHEAD: Impact on War Cinema

movies.title: Stop-Loss
movies.slug: A decorated Iraq War veteran faces being forcibly returned to active duty through the military's stop-loss policy

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond military themes, helping establish a new wave of socially conscious thrillers like Rendition (2007) and Body of Lies (2008). Its unflinching look at institutional failure and cover-ups shares DNA with films like Standard Operating Procedure (2008) and Green Zone (2010), which similarly questioned official narratives about the Iraq War.
